propositions.text: The Appeal Division decided that the Canada Employment Insurance Commission could not reconsider Ms. Emamifar’s claim more than 36 months after last payment.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division decided that the Canada Employment Insurance Commission (Commission) could not reconsider Ms. Zahra Emamifar’s claim for parental benefits under the Employment Insurance Act, S.C. 1996, c. 23 (the Act) more than 36 months after those benefits had last been paid to her.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded that the condition for extending reconsideration beyond 36 months was not met because there was no evidence of false or misleading information.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division concluded that this condition had not been met because there was no evidence that the information Ms. Emamifar provided in her application for parental benefits was false or misleading and her failure to inform the Commission that she had returned to work and received earnings was an omission that did not qualify as a statement or representation.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division decided it could not extend the reconsideration period because there was no false or misleading information.

propositions.text: The Court can only set aside the decision if it exhibits significant flaws and is not justified, intelligible, or transparent.
propositions.quote: This Court can set aside the Decision only if the Attorney General establishes that it exhibits shortcomings or flaws sufficiently central or significant such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility, and transparency.

propositions.text: The Court's role is to assess whether the decision is reasonable, not what decision it would have made.
propositions.quote: In assessing whether the Decision is reasonable, it is not the role of this Court to ask what decision it would have made in place of that made by the Appeal Division.

propositions.text: The Court will only intervene if the decision shows significant flaws.
propositions.quote: This Court can set aside the Decision only if the Attorney General establishes that it exhibits shortcomings or flaws sufficiently central or significant such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility, and transparency.

paragraphs.summary: The Court reviews the decision for reasonableness, not to replace it, and only if it has significant flaws.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar applied for parental benefits effective October 6, 2019, expecting to return to work on April 3, 2021.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar applied for maternity and parental benefits under the Act effective October 6, 2019, indicating on her application that she expected to return to work with her employer 18 months later, on April 3, 2021.

propositions.text: Her employer issued an electronic record of employment with an expected return date of April 2, 2021.
propositions.quote: On October 17, 2019, her employer issued an electronic record of employment (ROE) with April 2, 2021, as her expected date of recall, consistent with an 18-month absence from work.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar applied for benefits expecting to return to work in April 2021, and her employer issued an ROE with that date.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar sought to be exempted from reporting every two weeks, agreeing to an exemption declaration.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar selected “yes”, indicating her agreement with the statements set out in the exemption declaration.

propositions.text: The exemption declaration stated she would not need to complete reports if she agreed.
propositions.quote: I understand that I am making a claim for benefits covering every week of my period of eligibility and I accept that I will not be required to complete reports for this period.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar agreed to an exemption from biweekly reporting in her application.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar selected “yes” to the exemption declaration, indicating her agreement.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar selected “yes”, indicating her agreement with the statements set out in the exemption declaration.

propositions.text: She read and accepted her rights and responsibilities in the application.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar also sought to be exempted from reporting every two weeks in order to receive her employment insurance (EI) benefits (the reporting exemption). The online application contained the following “Exemption Declaration”: Exemption Declaration – Maternity/Parental Answers to fields and questions with an asterisk (*) are mandatory. Normally you are asked to complete a report every two weeks to receive your EI payment. Each completed report becomes a claim for benefits for the weeks of unemployment. You could be exempted from completing reports. Before being exempted, you must agree to the following statement. I understand that I am making a claim for benefits covering every week of my period of eligibility and I accept that I will not be required to complete reports for this period. I also agree to inform Service Canada immediately if, while I am collecting Employment Insurance benefits • I work, • I receive money, or • any situation arises that affects my Employment Insurance benefits. Following receipt of my last payment of benefits, I agree to notify Service Canada to confirm that I have declared any situation or earnings that have the effect of reducing or eliminating my benefits. I am aware that I may be penalized or subject to prosecution for failing to report any of the above. * I agree to the above statements and wish to be exempted from completing reports. ○ Yes ○ No

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar agreed to the exemption and read her rights and responsibilities.

propositions.text: The “Rights and Responsibilities” section specified that employment earnings must be accurately reported.
propositions.quote: Another section of the online application, titled “Rights and Responsibilities,” specified, among other things, that “[w]hen requesting maternity or parental benefits, you must… accurately report all employment earnings… in the week(s) in which they were earned” (emphasis in the original).

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement acknowledging she read and accepted her rights and responsibilities.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement that she had read, understood and accepted her rights and responsibilities.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar acknowledged reading and accepting her reporting responsibilities.

propositions.text: The “Attestation” section stated she declared her information was true to her knowledge.
propositions.quote: Finally, the “Attestation” section of the online application stated in part: “I declare that the information given to the questions on the Application for Employment Insurance benefits online and questionnaires is true to the best of my knowledge.”

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement accepting the attestation.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar checked a statement that she accepted the attestation.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar attested that her information was true and accepted the attestation.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar returned to work earlier than expected, and her employer submitted a revised ROE indicating her return in October 2020.
propositions.quote: However, Ms. Emamifar returned to work earlier than she had expected. Her employer submitted to Service Canada a revised electronic ROE dated October 21, 2020, indicating that she had returned to work in October 2020.

propositions.text: She did not inform the Commission of her return or earnings but continued receiving benefits until March 27, 2021.
propositions.quote: Ms. Emamifar did not inform the Commission that she had returned to work or was receiving employment income. She continued receiving parental benefits until March 27, 2021.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar returned to work early, but did not inform the Commission and continued benefits until March 2021.

propositions.text: The Commission sent a notice of decision in July 2024, alleging she made a false or misleading statement by not declaring income.
propositions.quote: On July 31, 2024, the Commission sent a notice of decision to Ms. Emamifar stating that it was of the opinion that a false or misleading statement or representation had been made because she had failed to declare employment income.

propositions.text: The notice was sent more than 36 months after her last benefit payment.
propositions.quote: Significantly, this notice of decision was sent more than 36 months following the last payment of Ms. Emamifar’s benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The Commission issued a decision in 2024 alleging false statements, over 36 months after last benefits.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar explained she thought her benefits were normal and that her employer would notify the Commission.
propositions.quote: She explained to the Commission that she had originally intended to be off work for 18 months, but that she had to return to work after 12 months when her spouse was laid off during the COVID pandemic. She said that she had assumed that she had been approved for a lump sum with the option to have the benefits paid over 12 or 18 months and that she had believed that the continuing benefit payments were normal since she had already been approved for the entire amount of benefits. She also explained that she had expected her employer to notify the Commission of her return to work.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar believed her benefits were normal and her employer would notify the Commission.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar appealed the reconsideration denial to the SST General Division.
propositions.quote: She also explained that she had expected her employer to notify the Commission of her return to work.

propositions.text: The Commission denied her reconsideration request, leading to her appeal to the SST General Division.
propositions.quote: The Commission denied Ms. Emamifar’s request for reconsideration, and she appealed to the General Division of the SST.

paragraphs.summary: Ms. Emamifar appealed after her reconsideration was denied.

propositions.text: The Commission argued her failure to report her return and earnings was a false statement, based on her agreement to the reporting conditions.
propositions.quote: The Commission submitted to the General Division that Ms. Emamifar’s failure to report her return to work and her earnings was an “omission of information” that constituted a false statement because she had agreed to the conditions for securing a reporting exemption in her application for benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The Commission argued her failure to report was a false statement based on her agreement.

propositions.text: The General Division allowed her appeal, finding the Commission relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to reconsider her claim.
propositions.quote: The General Division allowed Ms. Emamifar’s appeal (Z. E. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2025 SST 856 (GD Decision)). It found that the Commission had relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to reconsider her claim.

propositions.text: It noted that paragraph 38(1)(a) allows penalties for false or misleading representations, but the Commission did not impose a penalty.
propositions.quote: It found that the Commission had relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to reconsider her claim. That provision empowers the Commission to impose a penalty on a claimant in certain circumstances, including where the claimant made a representation that the claimant knew was false or misleading, or knowingly failed to declare earnings for a period in which the claimant claimed benefits. As the Appeal Division later recognized in the Decision, the Commission did not impose a penalty on Ms. Emamifar.

paragraphs.summary: The General Division found the Commission relied on a paragraph that involves penalties, but no penalty was imposed.

propositions.text: The General Division noted the law limits reconsideration to 36 months unless false or misleading statements are involved, which can extend to 72 months.
propositions.quote: It noted that under subsections 52(1) and (5) of the Act, the Commission has 36 months after benefits have been paid to reconsider a claim, or 72 months if it is of the opinion that a claimant has made a false or misleading statement or representation.

propositions.text: It adopted the reasoning that a “representation” requires action, not omission, based on J. S. and B. S. decisions.
propositions.quote: It adopted the reasoning of the Appeal Division in J. S. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2017 SSTADEI 431 at paragraph 13 [J. S.] that a “representation requires action, whether in verbal, written, visual, or other form”, and does not include an omission, such as a failure to report.

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar did not make statements or representations about her return or earnings because she was exempted from reporting.
propositions.quote: It found that Ms. Emamifar had “made no statements or representations about her return to work and earnings because she was exempted from completing the reports where she would otherwise have done so” (GD Decision at para. 39).

propositions.text: Therefore, the Commission could not extend the period to reconsider her claim.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, the General Division concluded that, since the Commission could not establish that Ms. Emamifar had made false or misleading statements, it had no authority to extend the period to reconsider her claim for benefits.

paragraphs.summary: The law limits reconsideration to 36 months unless false statements are involved, which can extend to 72 months, but omissions are not considered statements.

propositions.text: The Commission appealed the General Division’s decision.
propositions.quote: The Commission appealed the General Division’s decision to the Appeal Division.

paragraphs.summary: The Commission appealed the decision to the Appeal Division.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division agreed the General Division erred in relying on paragraph 38(1)(a) and clarified the authority is under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division agreed with the Commission that it had not imposed a penalty on Ms. Emamifar, and that the General Division had thus erred in concluding that the Commission had relied on paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act to extend the period for reconsideration of Ms. Emamifar’s claim to 72 months. Rather, the authority to extend the reconsideration period beyond 36 months is in subsection 52(5) of the Act.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division substituted its own decision for the General Division’s due to an error of law.
propositions.quote: Having found an error of law, the Appeal Division decided to substitute its own decision for that of the General Division rather than sending the file back.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found the law was misapplied and replaced the decision.

propositions.text: The Commission argued Ms. Emamifar agreed to her reporting responsibilities, and her failure to comply misled the Commission.
propositions.quote: The Commission submitted that Ms. Emamifar had agreed to the responsibilities set out in the online application, including the obligation to report all her earnings in the week they were earned. The Commission further submitted that, because Ms. Emamifar had failed to comply with her reporting obligations when she returned to work early, the Commission had been misled into paying her benefits and it was reasonable for the Commission to come to the opinion that her failure to inform was a false or misleading statement or representation (Decision at para. 38).

paragraphs.summary: The Commission argued her non-compliance with reporting obligations misled them.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division noted that failing to report is an omission, not a statement or representation, and thus does not extend the period.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division noted that in faulting Ms. Emamifar for failing to report to the Commission her return to work and her earnings, the Commission was describing an omission. The Appeal Division decided that failure to report information (an omission) did not constitute a statement or representation for the purpose of subsection 52(5), based largely on an analysis of the text of subsection 52(5), a comparison of that provision with paragraph 38(1)(a) of the Act, and the reasoning set out in J. S. and in a decision of the General Division in B. S. v. Canada Employment Insurance Commission, 2024 SST 469 [B. S.].

propositions.text: Ms. Emamifar’s exemption from filing reports meant she made no action or statement.
propositions.quote: Considering that Ms. Emamifar was exempt from filing biweekly reports, the Appeal Division found that she had taken no action and thus made no representation.

propositions.text: Therefore, the Commission could not extend the reconsideration period.
propositions.quote: Therefore, it concluded, the Commission could not extend the reconsideration period from 36 to 72 months and reconsider Ms. Emamifar’s claim.

paragraphs.summary: Omissions, like failure to report, do not qualify as statements, so the law does not extend the reconsideration period.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found Ms. Emamifar's information was accurate and truthful at the time of her application and that she made no action or representation.
propositions.quote: it saw no evidence that the information she provided in her application was false or misleading as it was accurate and truthful at the time she made her application

propositions.text: The Appeal Division interpreted 'representation' as requiring a verbal, written, visual or other form of action, excluding omissions.
propositions.quote: adopted the interpretation of “representation” in J. S., requiring a verbal, written, visual or other form of action

propositions.text: Since Ms. Emamifar was exempt from filing reports, she took no action and made no representation, so the reconsideration period could not be extended.
propositions.quote: she had taken no action and thus made no representation. Therefore, it concluded, the Commission could not extend the reconsideration period

propositions.text: Whether the Appeal Division's interpretation of 'representation' and its conclusion about the extension of the reconsideration period were reasonable.
The court reviews the Appeal Division’s decision under the reasonableness standard, focusing on its justification and rationality.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division’s decision, including its interpretation of the Act, is reviewable on the deferential standard of reasonableness

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires the decision to be based on a coherent, rational analysis justified by the facts and law.
propositions.quote: a reasonableness if it is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker

propositions.text: The court finds no merit in the argument that the failure to submit reports constitutes a statement or representation.
propositions.quote: There is no merit to this argument. In B. S., the General Division relied on the CUB decisions to conclude that the failure to submit reports cannot be considered “a statement or representation”

propositions.text: The Attorney General failed to meet its burden to show the decision was unreasonable, as it did not identify significant flaws.
propositions.quote: the Attorney General has failed to meet its burden

propositions.text: The court dismisses the application for judicial review and does not order costs since Ms. Emamifar did not participate.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss this application for judicial review. Since Ms. Emamifar did not participate in the proceedings, I would not order costs.

paragraphs.summary: The Appeal Division found Ms. Emamifar's information was truthful and that she made no action or representation, leading to a conclusion on the reconsideration period.

propositions.text: The challenger must show the decision is unreasonable, with flaws that are central or significant, not superficial.
propositions.quote: such shortcomings or flaws cannot be merely superficial or peripheral to the merits of the decision; they must be sufficiently central or significant to render the decision unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court states the burden on the applicant to prove the decision's unreasonableness, focusing on significant flaws.

propositions.text: The court must examine the written reasons holistically and contextually, not expecting perfection.
propositions.quote: Reasons must not be assessed against a standard of perfection; the fact they don’t include all the arguments, statutory provisions, jurisprudence or other details is not by itself a sufficient basis for setting aside the decision

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes a holistic, contextual review of reasons, not perfection.

propositions.text: The court will address each of the five shortcomings alleged by the Attorney General.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General submits that the Appeal Division’s reasons disclose five shortcomings or flaws that render its decision unreasonable. I address each of these in turn.

paragraphs.summary: The court will analyze five alleged flaws in the decision.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division unreasonably concluded Ms. Emamifar made no statements or representations in her application.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division unreasonably concluded that the information, agreements and attestations contained in Ms. Emamifar’s online application for EI benefits were not statements or representations.

paragraphs.summary: The court considers whether the Appeal Division wrongly found no statements in the application.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division considered the information in the online application as a statement or representation.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division considered the information supplied by Ms. Emamifar in her online application, including her responses agreeing to the attestation and statement of responsibilities, to be a statement or representation within the meaning of subsection 52(5)

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appeal Division viewed the application responses as statements.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division found no evidence that Ms. Emamifar made any statement or representation after filing her application.
propositions.quote: There is “no evidence that [Ms. Emamifar] made any statement or representation to the Commission at all”

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the Appeal Division's finding of no post-application statements.

propositions.text: The Attorney General argues that the statements in the application were truthful at the time, but she later failed to follow through.
propositions.quote: if a person says they will do something and then fails to do so, that is a reasonable basis to form the opinion that a false or misleading statement has been made.

paragraphs.summary: The Attorney General claims initial truthfulness but later failure to act indicates falsehood.

propositions.text: The court discusses the context of Dussault, where reporting exemptions are only for special benefits, not regular EI benefits.
propositions.quote: reporting exemptions are only available for special benefits under the Act, such as maternity or parental benefits. The exemptions are not available for ordinary EI benefits, such as those at play in Dussault.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the context of reporting exemptions in Dussault.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division acknowledged that Ms. Emamifar did not make any false or misleading statements in her application.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division ... concluded that she didn’t follow through with her responsibilities to report that information to the Commission. And I don’t accept that the Claimant “misled” the Commission into paying her benefits either.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appeal Division's conclusion that no false statements were made.

propositions.text: The court observes the Appeal Division's approach aligns with prior decisions, focusing on direct questions and factual statements.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division’s approach is consistent with that taken by the General Division in B. S., a case raising similar facts that the Appeal Division referred to in its reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the approach consistent with prior case law on statements.

propositions.text: Statements in biweekly reports relate to facts at or before the time of reporting, while online application statements relate to future intentions.
propositions.quote: the statements made by a claimant in response to biweekly reports relate to facts regarding the claimant’s situation at or before the time the statements are made, including whether they are working, have earned income or are available to work.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes factual reports from statements of future intent.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division's reasons show it understood the difference between present facts and future intentions in statements.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division’s reasons demonstrate that it grasped the Commission’s argument that Ms. Emamifar’s failure to follow through on her stated intention showed that she had made false or misleading statements.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the reasons show understanding of the distinction between facts and intentions.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division concluded that failure to follow through on intentions does not prove the absence of that intention at the time of application.
propositions.quote: the fact Ms. Emamifar failed to carry out her expressed intention did not, in itself, establish that she did not actually possess that intention at the time she submitted her application.

paragraphs.summary: The court reports the conclusion that not acting on intentions does not negate their existence at the time.

propositions.text: The court disagrees with the Attorney General that the decision conflicts with Dussault's ruling on intention.
propositions.quote: In light of my previous discussion of Dussault, I disagree with the Attorney General that the Appeal Division’s decision is inconsistent with the Court’s holding that it is unnecessary to find intention when assessing whether a false or misleading statement might exist.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds no conflict with Dussault regarding intention.

propositions.text: The court discusses Langelier, where proof of payment was not established, but false statements were not found due to lack of knowledge.
propositions.quote: the existence of a false or misleading statement could not be objectively inferred from the evidence: Revenue Canada’s inability to find proof that the claimant had been paid, in a proceeding where the claimant could not participate, could not in itself contradict his statement of fact that he had been paid for a week’s work.

paragraphs.summary: The court reviews Langelier, where lack of proof did not prove false statements.

propositions.text: The court notes that Langelier held that proof of payment is not enough to establish a false statement without knowledge.
propositions.quote: a decision which, as in the case at bar, is based on the absence of any proof of payment does not by itself support a conclusion that no payment was made and that it is false to say that there was a payment.

paragraphs.summary: The court emphasizes that proof of payment alone does not establish falsehood without knowledge.

propositions.text: Justice Décary explained that subsection 52(5) is strict and proof must be clear, especially for overpayment recovery.
propositions.quote: It should be borne in mind that [s. 52(5)] is part of an “exceptional [system], which is a departure from the ordinary law” and must be “strictly construed”

paragraphs.summary: The court highlights the strict construction of subsection 52(5) and the need for clear proof.

propositions.text: The court notes that in Dussault, false or misleading statements could be inferred from facts, not necessarily proven knowingly.
propositions.quote: In Dussault, it could be objectively inferred that the claimant had made a false or misleading statement regarding his lack of earnings, because the evidence showed that he was receiving self-employed income at the same time as he declared that he was not.

paragraphs.summary: The court discusses Dussault, where inference of falsehood was based on facts.

propositions.text: The court explains that in this case, the Appeal Division found no evidence that Ms. Emamifar’s statements were false, as they were consistent with her intentions at the time.
propositions.quote: the Appeal Division essentially concluded that the existence of a false or misleading statement could not be objectively inferred from evidence that Ms. Emamifar had not followed through on her stated intention, because that evidence did not contradict the statement made in her application.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Appeal Division's conclusion that no false statement was proven from the evidence.

propositions.text: The court observes the Appeal Division's approach aligns with prior decisions, focusing on direct questions and factual statements.
propositions.quote: The Court’s views on the role of intention originated in Canada (Attorney General) v. Langelier, 2002 FCA 157 [Langelier], on which Dussault relies.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the approach consistent with prior case law on statements.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division applied the implied exclusion rule but it was not improper in this case.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the Appeal Division’s reliance on implied exclusion was improper in this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the Appeal Division used the implied exclusion rule but finds this was not improper.

propositions.text: Implied exclusion is a textual argument that must be considered with purpose and scheme of the statute.
propositions.quote: the words of the statute must be considered in conjunction with its purpose and its scheme

propositions.text: Implied exclusion was not the sole basis for the interpretation; the Appeal Division also considered decisions on the meaning of 'representation'.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division also referred to SST decisions that focused on the meaning of the word “representation”.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes that implied exclusion is a textual argument but was not the only basis for the interpretation, as other decisions were considered.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division considered the purpose of the Act and subsection 52(5) and did not ignore it.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division relies on decisions of this Court which dealt with the purpose and operation of another predecessor to section 52 of the Act.

propositions.text: The purpose of section 52(5) is to give the Commission discretion to reconsider claims within time limits.
propositions.quote: The Commission has the statutory authority under s.52(5) to retroactively determine that benefits have been improperly paid and to ask for repayment.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division considered the purpose of the Act and subsection 52(5) and did not ignore it.

propositions.text: The interpretation of 'false and misleading statement or representation' was consistent with the purpose of the Act.
propositions.quote: In interpreting the words “false and misleading statement or representation”, the Appeal Division was aware that the Act aims to provide benefits but also to limit reconsideration within time limits.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division understood that the time limits depend on whether the Commission reasonably believes a false statement was made.
propositions.quote: section 52 contemplates that, in circumstances where the Commission has failed to reconsider a claim within 36 months... the claimant may keep benefits.

propositions.text: The Attorney General did not prove that the Appeal Division ignored or was inconsistent with the purpose of the Act.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General failed to meet this burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the Appeal Division correctly interpreted the purpose and scope of section 52(5) and did not ignore key elements.

propositions.text: Whether the Appeal Division asked the correct question under subsection 52(5).
propositions.quote: The Court’s decisions in Langelier and Dussault: whether the Commission had a reasonable basis to form the opinion.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division summarized the standard and set it out clearly in its reasons.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division accurately summarized the Commission’s submissions on the appropriate standard to apply under subsection 52(5).

propositions.text: The Appeal Division implicitly found no reasonable basis for the Commission to believe Ms. Emamifar made a false statement.
propositions.quote: Given its findings that there was no evidence the information Ms. Emamifar provided was false or misleading, the Appeal Division found no basis for the opinion.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the Appeal Division applied the correct standard and implicitly found no reasonable basis for the Commission's opinion.

propositions.text: The Appeal Division relied on a non-binding decision that itself relied on irrelevant decisions, but this was not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The Appeal Division expressed its agreement with the reasoning set out by the General Division in B. S. which, in turn, had relied on CUB decisions.

propositions.text: The CUB decisions involved penalties, which are not applicable here.
propositions.quote: the circumstances in which the Commission had assessed penalties against the claimant for making false statements or representations.

propositions.text: It was not unreasonable for the Appeal Division to adopt the reasoning of the General Division in interpreting the terms.
propositions.quote: It is not unreasonable for the Appeal Division to adopt the reasoning of the General Division in interpreting the meaning of these terms.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that relying on the General Division's reasoning, even if based on irrelevant decisions, was not unreasonable.

propositions.text: The Attorney General failed to show the decision was unreasonable by identifying significant flaws.
propositions.quote: The Attorney General bore the burden to show that it was unreasonable by identifying sufficiently central or significant shortcomings.

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is dismissed.
propositions.quote: I would dismiss this application for judicial review.

propositions.text: No costs are ordered since Ms. Emamifar did not participate.
propositions.quote: Since Ms. Emamifar did not participate in the proceedings, I would not order costs.

paragraphs.summary: The court dismisses the application for judicial review, noting no costs due to Ms. Emamifar's non-participation.
